node-loop-001.explanation: **The problem:** JavaScript runs on a single thread, so how can Node serve thousands of connections without blocking? **Why it works:** Node hands slow I/O (file reads, network, DNS) to the **system kernel** (and a small libuv thread pool for things the kernel can't do async), which work in the background. Node's single JS thread keeps running; when an operation finishes, its **callback is queued** to run on the JS thread via the event loop. **Why this scales:** the thread is almost never blocked waiting — it only runs your JS, which is fast, while the OS handles the waiting. **Common mistakes:** running CPU-heavy synchronous work on the main thread (it blocks *everything*, since there's only one JS thread) — offload that to worker threads or child processes.

resources.label: Node.js — Overview of Blocking vs Non-Blocking

node-loop-002.explanation: **The problem:** 'The event loop' sounds vague — it's actually a fixed sequence of **phases**, each with its own callback queue. **The order each iteration:** (1) **timers** — due `setTimeout`/`setInterval` callbacks; (2) **pending callbacks** — certain system I/O callbacks deferred from before; (3) **idle, prepare** — internal only; (4) **poll** — retrieve new I/O events and run their callbacks (Node **blocks here** when nothing else is pending); (5) **check** — `setImmediate` callbacks; (6) **close callbacks** — e.g. `socket.on('close')`. **Between every phase** (and between callbacks) Node drains the `nextTick` and microtask (Promise) queues. **Common mistakes:** assuming timers fire at exactly their delay (they fire in the timers phase *at or after* it), or confusing `setImmediate` (check) with `setTimeout(…,0)` (timers).

node-loop-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** Inside an I/O callback, `setTimeout(…,0)` vs `setImmediate` — what order? **The answer: immediate, then timeout — always.** **Why deterministic here:** the `fs.readFile` callback runs in the **poll** phase. From poll, the **check** phase (where `setImmediate` lives) comes *next*, before the loop wraps back around to the **timers** phase. So `setImmediate` always wins when both are scheduled from within an I/O callback. **Contrast:** at the *top level* of a script the order is non-deterministic (it depends on startup timing). **Common mistakes:** assuming the order is always the same regardless of context — it's only guaranteed when scheduled inside an I/O callback. **Rule of thumb:** to run 'right after this I/O callback', use `setImmediate`.

node-loop-003.explanation: **The problem:** Where does `process.nextTick()` fit among the event loop phases? **The answer: it's not part of the loop at all.** The `nextTick` queue is drained **immediately after the current operation finishes**, before the event loop is allowed to continue to the next phase — no matter which phase you're in. So nextTick callbacks always run before any timers, I/O, or `setImmediate`. **Why it exists:** to let you defer work to *right after* the current function unwinds (e.g. emit an event after the caller has attached listeners) without yielding to I/O. **Common mistakes:** assuming nextTick is 'the next loop iteration' (that's `setImmediate`), or recursively scheduling nextTick and starving I/O (see the starvation card).

node-loop-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** `function recursive() { process.nextTick(recursive); }` then calling it. **The danger: it starves the event loop.** Because the nextTick queue is fully drained *before* the loop may advance, endlessly re-queueing nextTick means the queue **never empties** — so Node never reaches the **poll** phase. All I/O (timers, network, file callbacks) is permanently blocked, even though the call stack doesn't overflow (each call returns before the next is scheduled). **Why not a stack overflow:** the recursion isn't synchronous — each `recursive` returns, then the queued one runs. **The fix:** use `setImmediate` to yield to the loop between iterations. **Common mistakes:** heavy recursive nextTick work, or assuming nextTick is throttled (it isn't).

resources.label: Node.js — process.nextTick and the event loop
Node.js — Don't block the event loop

node-loop-004.explanation: **The problem:** The names are admittedly backwards. **What each really does:** `process.nextTick()` fires the most **immediately** — right after the current operation, in the same phase, before the loop continues. `setImmediate()` fires on the **next** iteration of the event loop (the check phase). So despite the names, *nextTick* is sooner than *setImmediate*. **What the docs recommend:** prefer **`setImmediate`** in general — its 'run on the next loop tick' behavior is easier to reason about and it won't starve I/O the way recursive nextTick can. **Use `nextTick`** only when you specifically need to run before the loop proceeds (e.g. to fire an event after the caller attaches handlers). **Common mistakes:** reaching for nextTick by default and risking starvation.

node-loop-005.explanation: **The problem:** What's special about the **poll** phase? **The answer: it's where Node actually waits.** The poll phase has two jobs: run queued I/O callbacks, and **retrieve new I/O events**. When there are no timers due and nothing scheduled with `setImmediate`, the loop **blocks in poll** — sleeping efficiently until the OS reports new I/O (a socket readable, a file read done) or a timer becomes due. **Why this matters:** it's how a single-threaded runtime idles at ~0% CPU instead of busy-looping. If a `setImmediate` is pending, poll won't block (it ends so the check phase can run); if a timer is due, poll ends to service it. **Common mistakes:** thinking Node constantly spins the loop — it parks in poll when idle.

node-loop-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** At the **top level** of a script, `setTimeout(…,0)` vs `setImmediate` — what order? **The answer: unpredictable** — it depends on how fast the process starts up. **Why:** `setTimeout(fn, 0)` is clamped to a ~1 ms minimum. When the loop reaches the **timers** phase, whether that 1 ms has elapsed yet depends on how long startup took — so sometimes the timer is 'due' and runs first, sometimes it isn't and `setImmediate` (check phase) runs first. **Contrast:** inside an I/O callback the order *is* deterministic (immediate first), because you're already past the timers phase in poll. **Common mistakes:** relying on top-level ordering between these two; if you need a guaranteed order, schedule them from inside an I/O callback (or use one consistently).

node-loop-006.explanation: **The problem:** Does `setTimeout(fn, 0)` run `fn` right away? **The answer: no.** It **queues** `fn` to run in the **timers** phase of a *future* loop iteration — never synchronously. Before it runs: the rest of the currently executing code finishes, then the `nextTick` and Promise microtask queues drain, and possibly other phases execute. Also, `0` is clamped to a ~1 ms minimum delay. **Why:** `setTimeout` only *schedules*; it can't interrupt running code on the single thread. **When to use it:** to defer work to a later tick (yield to the loop), not to 'run now'. **Common mistakes:** expecting `setTimeout(fn,0)` to run before synchronous code after it, or using it to 'wait' for state that updates synchronously.

node-mod-001.explanation: **The problem:** In a CommonJS file you use `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename`, `__dirname` without ever declaring or importing them — where do they come from? **The answer:** before executing a module, Node wraps its source in a function: `(function (exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname) { … })`. Those five identifiers are the **parameters** of that wrapper, which is why they're available in every CJS module. **Why the wrapper:** it gives each module its own scope (top-level `var`s don't leak to global) and injects the module system's API. **Common mistakes:** assuming these are globals (they're module-scoped params — they don't exist in ES modules), or expecting `this` at top level to be `global` (in CJS it's `module.exports`).
node-mod-001.example:
```js
// These five identifiers exist because Node passes them into the module wrapper.
console.log(typeof require);     // 'function'
console.log(typeof module);      // 'object'
console.log(exports === module.exports); // true (they start as the same object)
console.log(__filename);         // absolute path to this file
console.log(__dirname);          // absolute path to its directory
```

node-mod-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** `exports = { hello: false }` — requiring this module yields an **empty object**, not `{ hello: false }`. **Why:** `exports` starts as a *reference* to `module.exports` (the same object). Node returns `module.exports`. Reassigning the local `exports` parameter just points that local variable at a new object — it **breaks the link** to `module.exports`, which is still the original empty object. So the require result is `{}`. **The fixes:** mutate it (`exports.hello = false`) to keep the link, or assign to `module.exports = { hello: false }` directly. **Why the others are wrong:** it's not `{hello:false}`, not undefined, and not read-only. **Common mistakes:** doing `exports = …` (reassign) instead of `module.exports = …` or `exports.x = …`.

node-mod-002.explanation: **The problem:** What does it mean that `require` **caches** modules? **The answer:** a module's top-level code runs **only once** — on the first `require`. Node stores the resulting `module.exports` in a cache keyed by the resolved file path, and every subsequent `require` of that same path returns the **same** cached object (no re-execution). **Why:** performance and shared singletons — config, DB connections, and counters are shared across all importers. **Implication:** mutating an exported object affects everyone who required it. **Cache key gotcha:** it's the *resolved path*, so case/symlink differences can create separate instances. **Common mistakes:** expecting side-effectful module code to run on every require, or relying on a module as a singleton across differently-resolved paths.

node-mod-003.explanation: **The problem:** How does `require('X')` decide what to load? **The resolution order:** (1) **core modules** (`fs`, `http`, `node:*`) win immediately; (2) for `./`, `../`, or absolute specifiers, treat `X` as a **file path**, trying `X`, then `X.js`, `X.json`, `X.node`; (3) if it's a **directory**, load its `package.json` `main` field, else `index.js`; (4) otherwise it's a **package name** — look in `node_modules` in the current directory, then walk **up** parent directories (`../node_modules`, `../../node_modules`, …) to the filesystem root. **Why the upward walk:** it lets nested packages share dependencies hoisted higher up. **Common mistakes:** expecting bare specifiers to resolve relative to the file, or forgetting the extension/`index.js` fallbacks.

node-mod-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** With no `type` field in `package.json`, which files are ES modules? **The answer: only `.mjs` files.** Without `"type": "module"`, `.js` defaults to **CommonJS**; `.mjs` is always ESM and `.cjs` is always CommonJS. If you set `"type": "module"`, then `.js` becomes ESM and you'd use `.cjs` for CommonJS. **Why explicit:** the extension/`type` field tells Node which module system to parse with — it does **not** sniff for `import` statements (that's why a stray `import` in a `.js` CJS file is a syntax error, not an auto-switch). **Why the others are wrong:** `.js` isn't ESM by default, ESM needs no bundler in Node, and there's no content-based fallback. **Common mistakes:** putting `import` in a `.js` file without configuring `type`/using `.mjs`.

node-mod-004.explanation: **The problem:** ES modules don't have `__dirname` or `__filename` (those are CommonJS wrapper params). **The replacement:** `import.meta`. Modern Node (20.11+/21.2+) exposes **`import.meta.dirname`** and **`import.meta.filename`** directly. On older versions, derive them from **`import.meta.url`** (a `file://` URL) using `fileURLToPath`. **Why the change:** ESM is spec-defined across environments and uses URLs, not OS paths, so path globals were replaced by `import.meta`. **Common mistakes:** using `__dirname` in an `.mjs`/`type:module` file (ReferenceError), or passing `import.meta.url` (a URL string) where a filesystem path is expected without converting it.

node-mod-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** An ESM file does `import cjs from './cjs.cjs'` where the CJS module did `module.exports = { name: 'exported', value: 42 }`. **What is `cjs`?** The **whole `module.exports` object** — `{ name: 'exported', value: 42 }`. **Why:** Node's interop maps a CommonJS module's `module.exports` to the ES module's **default export**, so the `import x from` (default) binding receives the entire exports object. **Note:** Node also tries to expose named exports via static analysis when it can detect them, but the default import always gives you the full `module.exports`. **Why the others are wrong:** CJS modules do get a default export (the exports object), it's not undefined, and import isn't a Promise (that's dynamic `import()`). **Common mistakes:** expecting named imports from a CJS module that only set `module.exports = {…}`.

node-mod-005.explanation: **The problem:** You need an `await`ed value (config, a dynamic import, a DB connection) available as a module's export, before any other code can run. **Top-level await (TLA):** using `await` directly at a module's top level, **outside** any `async` function. **Where it's allowed:** **ES modules only** — not CommonJS (whose synchronous `require` can't pause). When a module uses TLA, modules importing it wait for it to finish initializing. **Why useful:** clean async setup without an init function or IIFE. **The caveat:** it can delay the module graph's evaluation, so don't `await` slow things needlessly at module scope. **Common mistakes:** trying TLA in a `.cjs`/CommonJS file (syntax error), or creating slow import chains where one TLA blocks many importers.

node-mod-006.explanation: **The problem:** A file should behave differently when run directly (`node file.js`) versus when `require`d as a dependency (e.g. only start a server when run directly). **The check:** `require.main === module`. `require.main` is the module that was the entry point of the process; `module` is the current module. They're equal **only** when this file is the one Node started with. **Why useful:** lets a file both export reusable functions *and* have a runnable CLI/demo section. **ESM equivalent:** compare `import.meta.url` against the launched script (or use the newer `import.meta.main` where available). **Common mistakes:** running setup/`listen()` unconditionally at module top level, so requiring the file for its exports triggers unwanted side effects.

node-ev-001.explanation: **The problem:** You need a one-to-many notification system — emit 'something happened' and let any number of interested parties react. **The EventEmitter API:** register a listener with `.on(name, fn)`, and fire the event with `.emit(name, ...args)`. **Passing data:** every argument after the event name in `emit` is forwarded to each listener in order. **Why it's everywhere:** much of Node's core (streams, servers, processes) is built on EventEmitter — it's the backbone of the event-driven model. **Common mistakes:** typos in event names (listener silently never fires — names are just strings), forgetting that `emit` runs listeners synchronously, or emitting before listeners are attached.

node-ev-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** When you call `emit('event')`, how do the listeners run? **The answer: synchronously, in registration order** — `emit` invokes each listener one after another and does **not** return until they've all finished. **Why:** EventEmitter is a synchronous dispatch mechanism, not a queue; it's essentially calling an array of functions in order. **Implication:** a slow/throwing listener blocks the emit (and the thread); if you want async behavior, a listener can schedule its own work (e.g. `setImmediate`). **Why the others are wrong:** it's not deferred to the next loop iteration, not parallel (single thread), and not reverse order. **Common mistakes:** assuming `emit` is async, or relying on listener order across modules where registration timing is unclear.

node-ev-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** `emit('error', new Error('whoops!'))` with **no** `'error'` listener. **What happens: it throws and crashes the process.** **Why:** `'error'` is a special-cased event. If an EventEmitter emits `'error'` and there is no registered `'error'` handler, Node throws the error (and, being unhandled, it terminates the process). This is deliberate — silently swallowing errors would hide failures. **The fix:** always attach an `'error'` listener to emitters that can fail (streams, sockets, etc.). **Why the others are wrong:** it's not swallowed, not merely logged-and-continued, and `emit` doesn't quietly return false here. **Common mistakes:** forgetting the `'error'` handler on streams/servers, leading to crashes in production on the first error.

node-ev-002.explanation: **The problem:** Sometimes you want a listener to fire forever, sometimes exactly once, and you need to clean them up. **`on()` vs `once()`:** `on(name, fn)` runs `fn` on **every** matching emit; `once(name, fn)` runs it a **single** time, then auto-removes itself. **Removing listeners:** `emitter.off(name, fn)` (alias of `removeListener`) removes a specific listener — which means you must keep a **reference to the same function** you registered (an inline arrow can't be removed). `removeAllListeners(name)` clears them all for an event. **Why cleanup matters:** lingering listeners are a common memory leak (see the MaxListeners warning). **Common mistakes:** passing a different function reference to `off` (no-op), or never removing long-lived listeners.

node-ev-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** The warning 'MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 listeners added'. **What it means:** more than the **default limit of 10** listeners were registered for a *single* event on one emitter. It's a **warning, not a hard cap** — Node still adds the 11th — meant to flag a likely **leak**: listeners being added repeatedly (e.g. in a loop or on every request) without being removed. **What to do:** find and fix the duplicate registration / add cleanup; if you legitimately need more, raise the limit with `emitter.setMaxListeners(n)`. **Why the others are wrong:** it's not out-of-memory, not a hard limit that drops the 11th, and unrelated to emit count. **Common mistakes:** adding a listener inside a frequently-called function without removing it.

node-ev-003.explanation: **The problem:** What is `this` inside an EventEmitter listener? **The answer depends on the function type.** A **regular `function`** listener gets `this` bound to the **emitter instance** (so you can reach `this.eventNames()`, etc.). An **arrow function** ignores that binding — arrows capture `this` from their enclosing scope (in a module that's typically `module.exports`/`undefined`), because arrows never rebind `this`. **Why:** EventEmitter calls listeners with the emitter as the call-time `this`, but arrow functions have lexical `this` that can't be overridden. **Common mistakes:** using an arrow listener and expecting `this` to be the emitter, or relying on `this` at all (prefer closing over the emitter variable for clarity).

node-ev-004.explanation: **The problem:** You want to `await` the next occurrence of an event instead of using a callback. **The API:** the **`once` function** exported from `node:events` (not the `.once()` method): `const [value] = await once(emitter, 'myevent');`. It returns a Promise that resolves with an **array** of the emitted arguments when the event fires. **Error handling:** if the emitter emits **`'error'`** while you're awaiting, the promise **rejects** with that error — so wrap it in try/catch. **Why useful:** lets event-based APIs participate in async/await flows cleanly. **Common mistakes:** confusing the `once` function with the `.once()` method, forgetting the result is an array of args, or not handling the rejection path.

node-fs-001.explanation: **The problem:** File I/O has different needs — async in servers, simple scripts, startup config. **`fs` offers three API styles:** (1) **Promise-based** (`node:fs/promises`) — `await readFile(path, 'utf8')`; the modern default for async code. (2) **Callback** (`node:fs`) — `readFile(path, 'utf8', (err, data) => …)`; the classic error-first style. (3) **Synchronous** — `readFileSync(path, 'utf8')`; blocks until done. **Which to use:** prefer the Promises API in app code; sync only for startup/CLI scripts where blocking is fine; callbacks for legacy/hot paths. **Note:** passing an encoding (`'utf8'`) returns a string; omit it to get a `Buffer`. **Common mistakes:** using `readFileSync` in request handlers (blocks the loop), or forgetting the encoding and getting a Buffer.

node-fs-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** Why avoid `readFileSync` inside an HTTP request handler? **The answer: it blocks the event loop** — while the synchronous read runs, the single JS thread can do nothing else, so **no other request is processed** until it finishes. Under load this serializes all requests behind each file read, destroying throughput. **The fix:** use the async `fs.readFile`/`fs.promises.readFile` so the thread keeps serving other requests while the OS does the read. **Why the others are wrong:** there's no 64 KB limit, it's not deprecated, and it returns a string/Buffer that's perfectly sendable. **Where sync IS fine:** one-time startup/config reads before the server starts accepting traffic. **Common mistakes:** any synchronous I/O (sync fs, `execSync`, heavy CPU) on the request path.

resources.label: Node.js — Don't Block the Event Loop

node-fs-002.explanation: **The problem:** Node's classic callback APIs need a consistent way to report failures. **The error-first convention:** the callback's **first** parameter is reserved for an error — `(err, data) => …`. On success, `err` is `null`/`undefined` and the remaining args hold the result; on failure, `err` is an `Error` and the other args are **unreliable** (often undefined). So you **check `err` first** before using the data. **Why a convention:** with no exceptions across async boundaries, a uniform signature lets every callback API handle errors the same way. **Common mistakes:** ignoring `err` and using `data` regardless (crashes on null), throwing inside the callback without handling, or assuming a thrown error from async code can be caught with try/catch around the call (it can't).

node-path-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** `path.join('foo','bar')` vs `path.resolve('foo','bar')` from cwd `/home/myself/node`. **The answers:** `join` → **`'foo/bar'`** (just joins the segments with the separator — a *relative* path); `resolve` → **`'/home/myself/node/foo/bar'`** (resolves to an **absolute** path, starting from the current working directory when given relative segments). **Why the difference:** `join` concatenates/normalizes path pieces; `resolve` processes segments right-to-left until it builds an absolute path, prepending `process.cwd()` if needed. **Why the others are wrong:** they don't both return the same thing. **Rule of thumb:** `join` to build a relative sub-path; `resolve` when you need an absolute path. **Common mistakes:** expecting `join` to make paths absolute, or that `resolve` keeps things relative.
node-path-mcq-001.example:
```js
const path = require('node:path');
// Assuming process.cwd() is /home/myself/node:
console.log(path.join('foo', 'bar'));    // 'foo/bar'                (relative)
console.log(path.resolve('foo', 'bar')); // '/home/myself/node/foo/bar' (absolute)
console.log(path.resolve('/a', 'b'));    // '/a/b' (leading / makes it absolute)
```

node-path-001.explanation: **The problem:** Building paths with string concatenation (`'/foo/bar/' + filename`) breaks across platforms and on edge cases. **Why `path.join` is better:** **cross-platform correctness** — Windows uses `\` as the separator, POSIX uses `/`. `path.join` picks the right separator for the OS and **normalizes** the result (collapsing duplicate slashes, handling `..`/`.`). String concatenation hard-codes one platform's convention and can produce `//` or wrong separators. **Why it matters:** the same code then runs correctly on Linux servers and Windows dev machines. **Common mistakes:** manual `'/'` concatenation, mixing separators, or not normalizing user-supplied path segments (also a traversal risk — validate those).

node-path-002.explanation: **The problem:** Pulling the filename, directory, or extension out of a path by hand (splitting on `/`) is error-prone. **The helpers** for `/foo/bar/quux.html`: `path.basename` → **`'quux.html'`** (the last segment; pass a suffix like `'.html'` to strip it → `'quux'`); `path.dirname` → **`'/foo/bar'`** (everything but the last segment); `path.extname` → **`'.html'`** (the extension, including the dot). **Why use them:** correct across separators and edge cases (no extension, trailing slashes, dotfiles). **Common mistakes:** manual string slicing, forgetting `extname` includes the dot, or assuming `basename` strips the extension by default (it doesn't unless you pass the suffix).
node-path-002.example:
```js
const path = require('node:path');
const p = '/foo/bar/quux.html';

console.log(path.basename(p));         // 'quux.html'
console.log(path.basename(p, '.html'));// 'quux' (suffix stripped)
console.log(path.dirname(p));          // '/foo/bar'
console.log(path.extname(p));          // '.html' (includes the dot)
```

node-proc-001.explanation: **The problem:** Reading inputs from the command line and the environment. **Command-line arguments — `process.argv`:** an array where `[0]` is the **node executable path**, `[1]` is the **script path**, and the **real arguments start at index 2**. So slice from 2 to get user args. **Environment variables — `process.env`:** a plain object mapping variable names to **string** values (everything is a string; `undefined` if unset). **Why:** these are the standard channels for configuring a process at launch. **Common mistakes:** forgetting to skip the first two `argv` entries, treating `process.env` values as non-strings (e.g. `process.env.PORT` is a string — convert with `Number`), or assuming a var exists without a fallback.

node-proc-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** `process.exit(1)` vs setting `process.exitCode = 1` and returning. **The difference:** `process.exit()` **terminates immediately** — it can cut off pending async work, including **unflushed stdout/stderr** (since writes to pipes can be async), so logs or output may be lost. Setting `process.exitCode = 1` instead lets the process **finish its work naturally** (drain I/O, run remaining callbacks) and then exit with that code. **Best practice:** prefer setting `exitCode` and letting the event loop empty; reserve `process.exit()` for when you truly must stop right now. **Why the others are wrong:** they're not identical, `exitCode` is cross-platform, and `exit(1)` doesn't restart anything. **Common mistakes:** `process.exit()` right after `console.log` (output may be truncated).

node-stream-001.explanation: **The problem:** `fs.readFile` loads the **entire** file into memory before your code sees a single byte — fine for small files, fatal for large ones (a 2 GB file needs 2 GB of RAM, and nothing happens until it's all read). **Why a stream is better:** it delivers the file in **chunks**, so memory use stays roughly **constant** regardless of file size, and processing can **start as soon as the first chunk arrives** (lower latency). **Why this matters:** servers handling big files or many concurrent transfers stay healthy. **Common mistakes:** using `readFile` for large/unbounded inputs (uploads, big logs), buffering a whole stream into a string just to process it, or ignoring backpressure when piping.

node-stream-002.explanation: **The problem:** 'Stream' is one word for several roles. **The four types:** **Readable** — a data **source** you read from (`fs.createReadStream`, `http.IncomingMessage`, `process.stdin`). **Writable** — a **sink** you write to (`fs.WriteStream`, `process.stdout`, `http.ServerResponse`). **Duplex** — both readable *and* writable, independent directions (`net.Socket`). **Transform** — a Duplex whose **output is computed from its input** (gzip, encryption, upper-casing). **Why know them:** they compose — read from a Readable, through Transforms, into a Writable. **Common mistakes:** confusing Duplex (two independent channels) with Transform (output derived from input), or trying to write to a Readable / read from a Writable.

node-stream-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** `a.pipe(b).pipe(c)` vs `pipeline(a, b, c, cb)`. **Why the docs recommend `pipeline()`:** it **propagates errors** across *all* connected streams and **cleans up** (destroys) every stream when any one fails or the pipeline completes. With plain `.pipe()`, if one stream errors, the others are **not** automatically destroyed — leaving dangling streams/file descriptors (a **leak**), and you'd have to wire `'error'` handlers on each stream manually. **Why the others are wrong:** pipeline isn't faster by skipping streams, `.pipe()` isn't deprecated, and `.pipe()` can chain many streams too. **Bonus:** `node:stream/promises` `pipeline` returns a Promise for clean `await`. **Common mistakes:** chaining `.pipe()` without per-stream error handling and leaking on failure.

node-stream-003.explanation: **The problem:** A fast producer can generate data quicker than a slow consumer (disk/network) can accept it — without throttling, data piles up in memory until it's exhausted. **Backpressure** is the flow-control mechanism that prevents this. **How the API expresses it:** when a Writable's internal buffer grows past its **`highWaterMark`**, `write()` returns **`false`**, signaling 'I'm full — stop'. The producer should **pause** and wait for the **`'drain'`** event before resuming. `pipe()`/`pipeline()` handle this for you automatically. **Why it matters:** it keeps memory bounded under load. **Common mistakes:** ignoring `write()`'s return value in manual loops (unbounded buffering), or hand-rolling piping instead of letting `pipe`/`pipeline` manage backpressure.

node-stream-004.explanation: **The problem:** Event/callback stream code (`.on('data')`, `.on('end')`) is verbose and easy to get wrong. **Modern consumption:** Readables are **async-iterable**, so you can `for await (const chunk of source)` to read chunks with normal control flow and try/catch. **Transforming with pipeline:** `pipeline` from **`node:stream/promises`** accepts **async generator functions** as transform stages — `yield` the transformed chunks — and returns a Promise you can `await`, with full error propagation and cleanup. **Why it's better:** linear, readable async code instead of nested event handlers. **Common mistakes:** mixing `for await` consumption with `.pipe()` on the same stream, or forgetting that the generator receives the source as its argument.

node-buf-001.explanation: **The problem:** JavaScript strings are for text (UTF-16), but I/O deals in raw **bytes** (images, network packets, compressed data). **What a `Buffer` is:** a fixed-length container of raw binary data living **outside** V8's string/heap world — essentially a `Uint8Array` with extra methods. **Where you meet one:** any time Node hands you I/O **without a declared encoding** — `fs.readFile` *without* `'utf8'`, stream `'data'` chunks, TCP `socket` data. **Working with it:** convert to text with `buf.toString('utf8')`, create with `Buffer.from(...)`, and index bytes directly. **Common mistakes:** assuming chunks are strings (they're Buffers unless you set an encoding), slicing a multi-byte UTF-8 character across chunk boundaries (corrupts it — use `StringDecoder` or decode the whole thing), or using the deprecated `new Buffer()`.
node-buf-001.example:
```js
const buf = Buffer.from('hí', 'utf8'); // raw bytes, not a JS string
console.log(buf);             // <Buffer 68 c3 ad> — 3 bytes ('í' is 2 bytes)
console.log(buf.length);      // 3 (bytes, not characters)
console.log(buf[0]);          // 104 (byte value of 'h')
console.log(buf.toString('utf8')); // 'hí' — back to text
```

node-stream-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** Serving a **2 GB** video. Which approach keeps the server healthy? **The answer:** `fs.createReadStream(file).pipe(res)` — it streams the file in **chunks** with automatic **backpressure**, so memory stays bounded and one request can't exhaust RAM. **Why the others fail:** `fs.readFile` (and `readFileSync`) load the **entire 2 GB into memory per request** — a handful of concurrent requests OOMs the server (and sync also blocks the event loop); caching a 2 GB file in memory on startup is even worse and doesn't scale to many files. **Bonus:** `pipe`/`pipeline` also stop reading when the client is slow (backpressure) and clean up on disconnect. **Common mistakes:** buffering large/unbounded responses, or using sync I/O on the request path.

node-http-001.explanation: **The problem:** You want an HTTP server without a framework, to understand what Express et al. build on. **The minimal recipe:** `http.createServer((request, response) => { … })` registers a handler that runs **for every request**; inside it you set the status (`response.statusCode`), headers (`response.setHeader`), and send the body + finish with `response.end(...)`. Then `server.listen(port)` starts accepting connections. **Why this is the core:** every Node web framework is sugar over this `(req, res)` model. **Common mistakes:** never calling `response.end()` (the request hangs), setting headers *after* writing the body (throws — headers go first on the wire), or doing blocking work in the handler.

node-http-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** Reading a POST body in raw Node requires collecting `'data'` chunks and concatenating on `'end'` — why so manual? **The answer:** the `request` object **is a Readable stream**. The body arrives in **chunks over the network**, not as a single ready value — so Node hands it to you incrementally, and you accumulate the chunks (Buffers) and join them once the stream ends. **Why streamed:** bodies can be large or slow; streaming keeps memory bounded and lets you reject oversized inputs early. **Why the others are wrong:** it's not rate-limiting, `request.body` doesn't exist in core Node (that's a framework/body-parser feature), and Buffers aren't packet-limited. **Common mistakes:** assuming `request.body` exists, not capping body size (DoS risk), or treating chunks as strings (they're Buffers).

node-http-002.explanation: **The problem:** Two ways to set the status + headers — when to use which? **`setHeader` + `statusCode`:** stage values individually; they're sent **implicitly** with the first body write (or `end`). Good when you build headers up across some logic. **`writeHead(200, {...})`:** sends the status line and all headers **explicitly, at once**. **The rule that applies to both:** headers must be set **before any body data** — on the wire the status line and headers come first, so once you've written body bytes you can't change them (attempting to throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`). **Note:** `writeHead` takes precedence and merges with anything previously `setHeader`'d. **Common mistakes:** calling `setHeader` after `write`/`end`, or calling `writeHead` twice.

node-err-001.explanation: **The problem:** Errors in Node arrive through **four** different channels, each needing a different handling style — mismatching them means errors slip through. **The four:** (1) **Synchronous throws** → wrap in **`try/catch`**. (2) **Error-first callbacks** → **check the first argument** (`if (err) …`). (3) **Promise rejections** → **`.catch()`** or **`try/catch` with `await`**. (4) **`'error'` events** on EventEmitters (streams, sockets, servers) → attach an **`'error'` listener** (unhandled `'error'` crashes the process). **Why it matters:** a `try/catch` won't catch an async callback error or a stream `'error'` event — you must use the channel that matches. **Common mistakes:** wrapping an async callback API in try/catch (won't catch it), or forgetting `'error'` listeners on streams.

node-err-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** Using `process.on('uncaughtException', err => log(err))` and **continuing to run**. **Official guidance:** treat `uncaughtException` as a **last resort** — **log the error, then exit and let a process manager restart** the app. After an uncaught exception, the app reached an unexpected state: resources may be half-released, invariants broken — so **resuming is unsafe** and can cause subtle corruption or leaks. **Proper use:** synchronous cleanup + `process.exit(1)`. **Why the others are wrong:** it's *not* the recommended resilience pattern; it *does* fire for sync throws that escape; and handling `unhandledRejection` too doesn't make continuing safe. **Common mistakes:** swallowing exceptions to 'keep the server up' (zombie process), instead of crashing cleanly and restarting (e.g. via PM2/systemd/k8s).

node-err-002.explanation: **The problem:** Branching on `error.message` to decide what went wrong. **Why use `error.code` instead:** `code` is a **stable, machine-readable** label (e.g. `'ENOENT'`) that's safe to compare against across Node versions and locales; `message` is **human-facing text** that can change between releases or be localized, so matching on it is brittle. **Common system error codes:** **`ENOENT`** = no such file or directory; **`EADDRINUSE`** = the address/port is already in use; **`ECONNREFUSED`** = the target refused the connection (nothing listening / blocked). **Why it matters:** reliable error handling (retry, fallback, user message) keys off `code`. **Common mistakes:** `if (err.message.includes('not found'))` (fragile), or ignoring `code` and treating all errors the same.

node-err-003.explanation: **The problem:** A low-level error (e.g. a socket failure) is too detailed for higher layers, but if you replace it with a friendly message you lose the root cause for debugging. **The `cause` option:** `new Error('Request failed', { cause: originalError })` **chains** errors — the new, domain-meaningful error carries the original on its **`error.cause`** property. **Why it's great:** callers see a clear high-level message, while logs/debuggers can still walk down to the underlying error (Node prints the cause chain in stack traces). **Standardized:** `cause` is part of the ES2022 `Error` spec. **Common mistakes:** swallowing the original error (re-throwing only a new message), or stuffing the cause into a custom property instead of the standard `cause` (tools won't display it).

node-exp-001.explanation: **The problem:** You need to run different code for `GET /`, `POST /users`, etc. **Express routing:** `app.METHOD(path, handler)` registers a handler for a specific HTTP method + path — `app.get('/', fn)`, `app.post('/users', fn)`, `app.put`, `app.delete`, and so on (METHOD is the lowercased HTTP verb). `app.all(path, fn)` matches **every** method for a path (handy for shared middleware on a route). **Why:** it maps the request's method+URL to your code declaratively. **The handler** receives `(req, res)` and must end the response. **Common mistakes:** forgetting to send a response (request hangs), mixing up method names, or defining a more general route before a specific one so the specific one never matches.

node-exp-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** Route `'/users/:userId/books/:bookId'` with `GET /users/34/books/8989` — what's `req.params`? **The answer:** `{ userId: '34', bookId: '8989' }` — an **object** keyed by the `:name` placeholders, with **string** values. **Why strings:** URL segments are text; Express doesn't guess types, so `'34'` is a string (convert with `Number(req.params.userId)` if you need a number). **Why not an array or merged string:** named params produce a keyed object, one entry per `:placeholder`. **Common mistakes:** assuming numeric params (then `req.params.userId === 34` is false), expecting an array, or forgetting to validate/parse params before using them in queries.

node-exp-002.explanation: **The problem:** A route can have **multiple** handler callbacks — how does control move between them? **The flow:** each handler gets `(req, res, next)`; calling **`next()`** passes control to the **next callback of the same route**. This lets you compose per-route steps (validate → authorize → handle). **`next('route')`:** a special form that **skips the remaining callbacks of the current route** and jumps to the **next matching route** entirely — useful to bail out of a route's chain based on a condition. **Note:** `next(err)` (any other argument) jumps to error-handling middleware. **Common mistakes:** forgetting to call `next()` (request hangs), calling `next()` *and* sending a response (double-send error), or confusing `next('route')` (skip to next route) with `next(err)` (error handler).

node-exp-003.explanation: **The problem:** Putting every route in one file doesn't scale. **`express.Router`:** a **mini-application** for modular routing — you define routes (and middleware) on a `router` object in its own file, then **mount** it under a path prefix with `app.use('/birds', router)`. The router's `'/'` and `'/about'` become `'/birds'` and `'/birds/about'`. **Why:** organizes a codebase by feature, keeps related routes + middleware together, and makes them reusable/testable. **Common mistakes:** forgetting to `module.exports` the router, mounting at the wrong prefix, or duplicating the prefix inside the router's own paths (e.g. defining `/birds/about` on a router already mounted at `/birds`).

node-exp-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** What does `app.route('/book')` enable? **The answer:** **chaining multiple method handlers for one path** — `app.route('/book').get(…).post(…).put(…)`. It returns a single route instance so you attach each HTTP method's handler in one fluent chain, avoiding repeating the path string and reducing typos. **Why use it:** cleaner grouping when one resource path supports several methods. **Why the others are wrong:** it doesn't register across all routers, doesn't generate CRUD automatically, and doesn't redirect. **Common mistakes:** repeating `app.get('/book')`, `app.post('/book')` separately (works, but more error-prone), or expecting `app.route` to do more than group handlers by path.

node-exp-004.explanation: **The problem:** Knowing which `res` method to use for each kind of response. **The main ones:** `res.send()` — send a body of various types (string/Buffer/object); `res.json()` — send JSON (sets `Content-Type: application/json`); `res.redirect()` — send a redirect (3xx + `Location`); `res.render()` — render a view template to HTML; `res.download()` — prompt the browser to download a file; `res.end()` — end the response with no body. **Why distinct:** each sets appropriate headers/status for its job. **Key rule:** end the cycle with exactly **one** terminating method per request. **Common mistakes:** calling two terminators (e.g. `res.send` then `res.json` → 'headers already sent'), using `res.send(obj)` vs `res.json(obj)` interchangeably (both JSON-ify objects, but `json` is explicit), or never ending the response.

node-mw-001.explanation: **The problem:** Cross-cutting concerns (logging, auth, parsing) shouldn't be copy-pasted into every route. **A middleware function** has access to `(req, res, next)` and runs during the request-response cycle. **The four things it can do:** (1) run **any code**; (2) **modify `req`/`res`** (e.g. attach `req.user`); (3) **end the cycle** by sending a response; or (4) call **`next()`** to pass control to the next middleware/route. An Express app is essentially an ordered **pipeline of middleware**. **Why:** composable, reusable request processing. **The cardinal rule:** a middleware must either end the response or call `next()` — otherwise the request **hangs**. **Common mistakes:** forgetting `next()`, or calling `next()` after already sending a response.

node-mw-mcq-001.explanation: **The problem:** A middleware logs the request, but the client hangs until timeout. **The bug:** the middleware **neither ends the response nor calls `next()`** — so control never leaves it, the routes are never reached, and the request stalls forever. **The rule:** every middleware must do exactly one of: send a response (ending the cycle) or call `next()` to continue. **The fix:** add `next()` after logging. **Why the others are wrong:** `console.log` doesn't block, `app.use` isn't method-specific, and you don't 'return res' to continue. **Common mistakes:** writing a logging/auth middleware and forgetting `next()`, or conditionally calling `next()` on some branches but silently doing nothing on others (those requests hang).

node-mw-002.explanation: **The problem:** Express middleware comes in several flavors; knowing them helps you organize an app. **The five types:** (1) **Application-level** — bound to the app with `app.use(fn)` or `app.METHOD(fn)`. (2) **Router-level** — the same, but on an `express.Router()` instance (`router.use(fn)`). (3) **Error-handling** — special **four-argument** `(err, req, res, next)` functions. (4) **Built-in** — shipped with Express: `express.static()`, `express.json()`, `express.urlencoded()`. (5) **Third-party** — installed packages like `cookie-parser`, wired via `app.use()`. **Why categorize:** each is registered/scoped differently. **Common mistakes:** putting error handlers anywhere but last, or forgetting that built-in body parsers must be registered before routes that read `req.body`.

node-mw-mcq-002.explanation: **The problem:** The app returns 401 for **every** request, even valid ones, because auth middleware is registered **before** the `/login` route. **Why:** middleware runs in **definition order**. `app.use(authMiddleware)` sits ahead of `app.post('/login')`, so every request — including the login request that's supposed to *issue* a token — hits auth first and is rejected. Nobody can ever obtain a token. **The fix:** register public routes (like `/login`) **before** the auth middleware, or scope auth to only the protected paths (`app.use('/api', authMiddleware)`). **Why the others are wrong:** it's not about `express.json()` ordering, `app.post` can follow `app.use`, and the param count isn't the issue. **Common mistakes:** applying global auth without carving out public endpoints.

resources.label: Express — Mounting middleware on a path

node-mw-003.explanation: **The problem:** How does Express know a middleware is for handling **errors**? **The signature:** an error-handling middleware takes **exactly four** parameters — `(err, req, res, next)`. That fourth `err`-first arity is how Express distinguishes it from regular middleware (you must include all four, even if you don't use `next`). **Where to register it:** **last** — after all other `app.use()` calls and routes — so it catches errors propagated (via `next(err)`) from anything above it. **Why last:** Express runs middleware in order and routes errors forward to the next error handler. **Common mistakes:** writing `(err, req, res)` (only 3 params — Express treats it as a normal middleware and it won't catch errors), or registering the error handler before the routes it should protect.

node-mw-mcq-003.explanation: **The problem:** In **Express 4**, a rejected promise inside an `async` route handler crashes the process instead of reaching your error handler. **Why:** Express 4 doesn't know about promises — it only forwards an error to error-handling middleware if you call **`next(err)`**. An unhandled rejection from an `async` handler isn't caught, so it becomes an unhandled rejection (and can crash). **The fixes:** wrap the handler in `try/catch` and call `next(err)` in the catch, or use a wrapper/`express-async-errors`. **Express 5** changes this — it **automatically** forwards rejected promises from async handlers to your error handler. **Why the others are wrong:** async handlers are allowed, `res.send` isn't the issue, and the missing `next` param isn't what disables error tracking. **Common mistakes:** assuming Express 4 catches async errors for you.

node-mw-004.explanation: **The problem:** An error happens **after** the response already started sending (e.g. mid-stream). Trying to send a fresh 500 page then throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. **Why check `res.headersSent`:** once headers (and possibly body) are on the wire, you **can't** start a new response — status/headers are already committed. So in your error handler, if `res.headersSent` is true, **delegate to Express's default handler** via `next(err)`, which closes the connection cleanly instead of crashing. Only render your custom 500 page when headers haven't been sent yet. **Why it matters:** prevents a secondary crash while handling the first error. **Common mistakes:** unconditionally calling `res.status(500).render(...)` in the error handler, which throws when a response is already in progress.

node-mw-005.explanation: **The problem:** Two of the most-used built-in middlewares. **`express.json()`:** parses incoming requests with a JSON body and puts the parsed object on **`req.body`** — without it, `req.body` is `undefined` for JSON POSTs. **`express.static('public')`:** serves static files (HTML, images, CSS, JS) directly from a directory, so a request for `/logo.png` returns `public/logo.png` with no route needed. **How used:** both are registered with `app.use(...)`, and (for body parsers) **before** routes that read `req.body`. **Why built-in:** these are so common Express ships them (no extra install). **Common mistakes:** reading `req.body` without registering `express.json()` first, registering the body parser after the route, or pointing `express.static` at the wrong folder.
